title: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
summary: Why ranking metrics cannot be optimized directly, the pointwise, pairwise and listwise families, RankNet's pair loss, LambdaRank's delta NDCG weighting, LambdaMART boosting on lambdas, and position bias in click data.
outcomes: Explain why NDCG has zero gradient almost everywhere and how pairwise and listwise surrogates get around it
Compute a RankNet pair probability, cost and gradient, and accumulate pushes per document
Compute a LambdaRank lambda as |delta NDCG| times the RankNet gradient and explain why it focuses on the top
Walk through one LambdaMART round: fit a tree to lambdas, set Newton leaf values, apply a learning rate
Configure query groups, label gain and truncation in LightGBM or XGBoost and correct click data for position bias

lessons.title: Why ranking needs its own loss function

blocks.md:
A search engine retrieves a few hundred candidate documents for a query and must put the best ones on top. From the ranking features course you have a **feature vector** for every (query, document) pair: BM25, click-through rate, freshness and so on. From the ranking metrics course you have **NDCG**, which rewards putting highly relevant documents near the top.

**Learning to rank** (LTR) learns a scoring function $f(x)$ that maps a feature vector to one number. At query time you score every candidate and sort by score, highest first.

Training data is grouped by query. Each **query group** is a list of documents for one query, each with a graded relevance **label**; Burges's overview uses five levels, $l \in \{0,1,2,3,4\}$. Labels are only comparable inside one group: a 2 for one query says nothing about a 2 for another.

The whole course uses one toy query with four documents. Their labels are A = 0, B = 2, C = 1, D = 0. Our current model (say, the first few trees of a model being trained) gives scores A = 2.0, B = 1.0, C = 0.5, D = 0.0. So it ranks A first, the one document nobody wants.

blocks.caption: The definitions used throughout (Burges, Eq. 5). The gain of a label is 2 to the label minus 1, so labels 0, 1, 2 have gains 0, 1, 3. The ideal DCG is the DCG of the list sorted by label.

blocks.title: The toy query under the current scores

scenes.caption: The model sorts by score: A, B, C, D. Positions are numbered from 1 on top.
Each position has a discount that shrinks with depth. DCG adds gain times discount: 0 + 3 x 0.6309 + 1 x 0.5 + 0 = 2.3928.
The ideal order is B, C, then A and D (both 0). Its DCG is 3 + 1 x 0.6309 = 3.6309, so NDCG = 2.3928 / 3.6309 = 0.6590.
Back to the model's order. The problem is visible: the label-0 document A holds position 1, the most valuable slot, and B is one position too low.

blocks.prompt: Suppose we keep B, C and D fixed and slowly lower A's score from 2.0 toward 0. How does NDCG change as $s_A$ decreases?
blocks.reveal: NDCG stays at exactly 0.6590 while $s_A > 1.0$, because the sorted order does not change. When $s_A$ drops below B's score of 1.0 it **jumps** to 0.9639 (order B, A, C, D), and below C's 0.5 it jumps again to 1.0000. Between the jumps it is perfectly flat, so its derivative with respect to the score is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jumps.

blocks.title: NDCG as a function of one document's score

scenes.caption: Flat at 0.6590 for every $s_A$ above B's score. Gradient descent on this curve gets a gradient of exactly 0 and never moves.
Move the slider: raising B's score moves the first step right. The steps sit at B's and C's scores, where A swaps with a document of a different label; passing D (also label 0) changes nothing.
This is the core difficulty Burges names: as functions of model scores, IR metrics are everywhere either flat or discontinuous, so plain gradient descent cannot optimize them.

blocks.md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes training the ranker by computing NDCG@10 on each batch and backpropagating through it. What happens?
options: Training works but is slower, because NDCG is expensive to compute
The gradient of NDCG with respect to the scores is zero almost everywhere, so the weights barely change
It works only if the labels are binary
It overfits, because NDCG uses the labels directly
blocks.explain: NDCG changes only when two documents swap order. Small score changes leave the sort, and therefore NDCG, unchanged, so the gradient is 0 (and undefined at the swap points). That is why LTR methods use a smooth surrogate or hand-designed gradients.

blocks.question: Why must LTR training data be grouped by query rather than treated as one big table of rows?
options: Because gradient boosting needs equal-size groups
Because the model needs the query text as a feature
Because labels and metrics only compare documents for the same query, so pairs and NDCG must be formed within a group
Because rows from different queries have different numbers of features
blocks.explain: A label of 2 for one query is not comparable to a 2 for another. Pairwise losses only pair documents of the same query, and NDCG is computed per query and then averaged.

blocks.md: Tie-Yan Liu's survey *Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval* sorts LTR methods into three families by what one training example is and what the loss looks at. All three still learn a scoring function $f(x)$ applied to one document at a time; they differ only in training.

blocks.title: Three ways to turn ranking into a loss

nodes.label:
loss over the
list or permutation

scenes.caption: Pointwise: each document is an independent example. Predict its label (regression) or its relevance class.
Pairwise: each example is two documents of the same query with different labels. The loss asks whether the more relevant one scores higher (RankNet, Ranking SVM).
Listwise: the example is the whole list for a query, and the loss is defined on the list (ListNet, ListMLE).

blocks.md:
**Pointwise** on our toy query: regress each score onto its label. The residuals (label minus score) are A: -2, B: +1, C: +0.5, D: 0. So the loss pushes hardest on A, which is right, but it also insists that C score exactly 1.0 and D exactly 0, even though only the order matters.

Liu lists the problems: the relative order between documents is never modeled, the position of a document in the list is invisible to the loss, and queries with many documents dominate the total loss.

**Pairwise** turns ranking into classification of pairs. Our query has 5 useful pairs: B over A, B over C, B over D, C over A and C over D. A and D share label 0, so that pair carries no preference and is skipped.

This models relative order directly, but Liu notes two weaknesses: every pair counts the same whether it sits at positions 1 and 2 or 50 and 51, and since the number of pairs can grow with the square of the number of documents, queries with many pairs dominate the loss.

**Listwise** losses look at the whole list. ListNet (Cao et al., 2007) turns scores into a probability for each document of being ranked first, using the Luce model; with the exponential transformation this is a softmax. It does the same for the labels and minimizes the cross entropy between the two distributions. (The full ListNet loss is over whole permutations, which costs m factorial terms, so the paper also gives a top-k version; top-one is the cheap case.)

blocks.tex: P_s(j) = \frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_k e^{s_k}}, \qquad L = -\sum_j P_y(j) \log P_s(j), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial s_j} = P_s(j) - P_y(j)
blocks.caption: ListNet top-one loss with the exponential transform. P_y uses the labels in place of the scores.

blocks.title: ListNet top-one probabilities on the toy query

scenes.caption: From the model scores (2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.0): A gets most of the top-one probability.
From the labels (0, 2, 1, 0): B should own most of it.
Cross entropy between them is 1.6583. The gradient P_s minus P_y pushes A down by 0.4967 and B up by 0.3972; D barely moves.

blocks.md: A common mix-up: these families describe the **training loss**, not the model. A listwise-trained model still scores each document independently at serving time, so serving cost is the same for all three.

LambdaRank and LambdaMART, the subject of the rest of this course, form their gradients from **pairs** but weight each pair by how much swapping it would change NDCG, which depends on the whole sorted list. They need RankNet first.

blocks.question: Under a pointwise squared-error loss, a document with label 0 that the model scores at 0.3 and that is ranked 80th still produces a gradient. Why is that a problem for ranking?
options: It is not a problem: every residual should be driven to zero
The loss spends effort on documents whose position users never see, because position is invisible to a pointwise loss
Squared error cannot be minimized by gradient boosting
The gradient has the wrong sign for label-0 documents
blocks.explain: Liu points out that pointwise losses ignore position, so they may overemphasize unimportant documents that are ranked low and never affect what users see.

blocks.question: Query Q1 has 10 documents and query Q2 has 200, each with mixed labels. With an unnormalized pairwise loss, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because pairs are formed per query
Q1 dominates, because its pairs are more informative
Q2 dominates, because it can contribute vastly more pairs, so the loss stops tracking the per-query average NDCG
The model cannot be trained because pair counts differ
blocks.explain: Pair counts can grow quadratically with documents per query, so a few big queries dominate a pairwise loss. Liu describes query-level normalization (dividing by the query's pair count) as the fix; LightGBM's lambdarank_norm also normalizes per query.

lessons.title: RankNet: a probability for every pair

blocks.md: **RankNet** (Burges et al., ICML 2005) was built at Microsoft Research for web search. The model can be anything whose output is differentiable in its parameters; the paper used a neural network. For a query, take each pair of documents $U_i, U_j$ with different labels and compute their scores $s_i = f(x_i)$ and $s_j = f(x_j)$. A sigmoid turns the score difference into the model's probability that $U_i$ should rank above $U_j$.

blocks.caption: The sigmoid parameter sigma sets how sharply the probability changes with the score gap. We use sigma = 1 throughout.

blocks.md: The cost is the cross entropy between $P_{ij}$ and the target probability. Write $S_{ij} = 1$ if $U_i$ is labeled more relevant, $-1$ if less, $0$ if tied; the target is $\bar P_{ij} = \tfrac12(1+S_{ij})$. Following Burges, list each pair once with the more relevant document first, so $S_{ij} = 1$ and the cost simplifies to the line below.

blocks.caption: RankNet cost for a pair where U_i should be above U_j (natural log).

blocks.title: RankNet probability and cost against the score gap

x.label: score gap s_i - s_j (i is more relevant)

scenes.caption: Pair B over A: the gap is s_B - s_A = -1.0, the wrong way round. P = 0.2689 and the cost is 1.3133.
At a gap of 0 the cost is ln 2 = 0.693, not 0: documents with different labels but equal scores are still pushed apart, a built-in margin.
Far right (correct order, big gap) the cost goes to 0. Far left (wrong order) it becomes linear in the gap, so badly misordered pairs keep a steady pull.
A larger sigma makes the sigmoid steeper and the cost turn linear sooner.

blocks.md: Differentiating the cost with respect to the scores gives the quantity everything else in this course is built on. Burges calls it $\lambda_{ij}$:

blocks.tex: \lambda_{ij} \equiv \frac{\partial C}{\partial s_i} = \frac{-\sigma}{1 + e^{\sigma(s_i - s_j)}} = -\frac{\partial C}{\partial s_j}
blocks.caption: Burges Eq. 3 with S_ij = 1. It is negative, meaning raising s_i lowers the cost. We will work with its size, the push, sigma / (1 + e^(sigma (s_i - s_j))).

blocks.md:
For B over A: push = 1 / (1 + e^(-1)) = 0.7311. B should go up by that much and A down by the same. Pairs already in the right order with a large gap give a push near 0.

**The factorization.** Rather than updating the weights after every pair, sum the contributions per document first: $\lambda_i = \sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in I} \lambda_{ij} - \sum_{j:\{j,i\}\in I} \lambda_{ji}$. With Burges's sign, $\lambda_i$ is negative for a document that should move up; the trace below tracks the push $-\lambda_i$, so positive means up. Then one backward pass per document suffices. Burges reports this took training time from close to quadratic in the number of documents per query to close to linear, and it is the observation that led to LambdaRank.

blocks.title: Accumulating RankNet pushes per document

scenes.caption: Start: every document's accumulated push is 0. Scores are the current model's.
Pair B over A: gap -1.0, push 0.7311. B gains it, A loses it.
Pair B over C: gap +0.5, push 0.3775. B gains it, C loses it.
Pair B over D: gap +1.0, push 0.2689. B gains it, D loses it.
Pair C over A: gap -1.5, push 0.8176. C gains it, A loses it.
Pair C over D: gap +0.5, push 0.3775. C gains it, D loses it.
Final RankNet pushes. A gets the largest push down, B the largest up. Note D: it gets a sizable push down even though it already sits in last place.

blocks.md: RankNet does not need graded labels, only a set of preferred pairs. Burges notes the pairs can even be inconsistent, for example from a confused judge who prefers U1 to U2, U2 to U3 and U3 to U1.

blocks.question: Two documents with different labels currently have identical scores. What is the RankNet cost of that pair (sigma = 1)?
options: 0, because the scores are not in the wrong order
ln 2, about 0.693, so the pair is still pushed apart
Infinite, because the probability is undefined
1, the maximum of the sigmoid
blocks.explain: At s_i = s_j the sigmoid gives P = 0.5 and C = ln(1 + e^0) = ln 2. Burges calls this a built-in margin: equal scores for differently labeled documents are still penalized.

blocks.question: A pair is correctly ordered with a gap of 6 (sigma = 1). Roughly how big is its push?
options: About 0.0025, close to zero
About 0.5
About 1, the maximum
Exactly 0
blocks.explain: Push = 1 / (1 + e^6) = 0.0025. Well-separated, correctly ordered pairs contribute almost nothing, so RankNet focuses on misordered or close pairs. It never reaches exactly 0.

lessons.title: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG

blocks.md: RankNet minimizes (a smooth version of) the **number of misordered pairs**. That is not what NDCG measures. Burges illustrates it with a list where moving the top result down three places and the bottom relevant result up five cuts pairwise errors from 13 to 11, yet makes the top of the list worse. RankNet's pushes grow with the number of pairwise errors a document is involved in; for NDCG we want the biggest pushes near the top.

**LambdaRank** (Burges, Ragno and Le, 2006) keeps RankNet's pair push and multiplies it by $|\Delta \mathrm{NDCG}|$: the change in NDCG if the two documents swapped rank positions with everything else fixed. It never writes down the loss first; it specifies the gradient directly, computed **after** sorting by the current scores, which sidesteps the flat and discontinuous metric.

blocks.caption: Burges Eq. 6. For NDCG a swap only changes the two documents' own terms, so the change is the gain difference times the discount difference at their current ranks r_i and r_j.

blocks.md: Worked pair, B over A. Currently A is at rank 1 and B at rank 2. Swapping them changes DCG by (3 - 0) x (1 - 0.6309) = 1.1072, so $|\Delta \mathrm{NDCG}|$ = 1.1072 / 3.6309 = 0.3049. The RankNet push was 0.7311, so the LambdaRank push is 0.7311 x 0.3049 = **0.2229**.

blocks.title: All five pairs: RankNet push times |delta NDCG|

scenes.caption: Each pair of differently labeled documents, with their current ranks. The pair A, D is absent because both have label 0.
The RankNet push depends only on the score gap. C over A is the most misordered pair (gap -1.5), so RankNet pushes it hardest.
|delta NDCG| depends on gains and positions. B over A involves rank 1 and the biggest gain gap, so swapping it matters most. C over D sits at ranks 3 and 4 with gains 1 and 0, so it barely matters.
The product. B over A now dominates at 0.2229, more than C over A at 0.1126, even though its RankNet push was smaller. C over D shrinks to 0.0072.

blocks.md: Accumulate per document exactly as before: each pair adds its lambda to the more relevant document's upward push and subtracts it from the other's. Because every pair adds equal and opposite amounts, the pushes in one query always sum to zero.

scenes.caption: Positive means push the score up, negative means push it down. Both methods agree on direction: B and C up, A and D down.
The sizes differ. With RankNet, D (already last) gets -0.646, almost as much as C. With LambdaRank, D gets only -0.0517: moving D cannot improve NDCG much.

blocks.prompt: Express each document's push as a share of the total push size in its method. Which document loses the most share when we switch from RankNet to LambdaRank?
blocks.reveal: D. Its share falls from 14.7% to 6.7%, and C's falls from 18.6% to 12.0%. A and B, the pair fighting over position 1, rise from 35.3% and 31.4% to 43.3% and 38.0%. LambdaRank concentrates effort where NDCG is decided: the top.

blocks.title: Share of total push, RankNet vs LambdaRank

scenes.caption: RankNet: the push is spread by how many misordered or close pairs each document is in.
LambdaRank: weighted by |delta NDCG|, the fight over position 1 (A and B) takes over 80% of the push.

blocks.md: Two more facts from Burges. First, LambdaRank was shown **empirically** to optimize NDCG directly: at the trained weights, random perturbations in weight space (459 random directions for 99% confidence) only lowered average NDCG. Second, to target another metric you replace $|\Delta \mathrm{NDCG}|$ by the change in that metric, such as MAP or MRR. XGBoost's `rank:map` objective is this swap.
A lambda is a RankNet pair gradient scaled by how much the metric would change if the pair swapped. Pairs that cannot change the top of the list get almost no weight.

blocks.question: You optimize NDCG@10. Two documents with very different labels sit at ranks 40 and 41. What is their lambda?
options: Large, because their labels differ a lot
Zero, because swapping two documents both below position 10 does not change NDCG@10
The RankNet push, unchanged
Negative for both documents
blocks.explain: With truncation at T = 10, positions beyond 10 contribute nothing to DCG@10, so swapping them changes NDCG@10 by 0 and the lambda is 0. Pairs need at least one document inside the top 10 to matter.

blocks.question: After computing lambdas for a query, a teammate finds the per-document pushes sum to 0.37. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing: sums vary from query to query
The query has more relevant than irrelevant documents
The learning rate is too high
There is a bug: each pair adds equal and opposite pushes, so the total must be 0
blocks.explain: Every pair contributes +lambda to one document and -lambda to the other, so the sum over a query is exactly zero (up to rounding).

lessons.title: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas

blocks.md:
**MART** (multiple additive regression trees, Friedman's gradient boosting) builds the model as a sum of small regression trees, $F_N(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i f_i(x)$. Each new tree is fit to the gradient of the cost with respect to the current scores at every training row, then added with a small step. MART never needs the cost itself, only those per-row gradients.

LambdaRank supplies exactly that: a gradient (the lambda) per document. **LambdaMART** is the combination. Burges notes that an ensemble of LambdaMART rankers won Track 1 of the 2010 Yahoo! Learning to Rank Challenge.

One boosting round, as in Burges's algorithm box:

1. Score every row with the current model, sort each query group, and compute each document's lambda $\lambda_i$ and weight $w_i$.
2. Fit a regression tree to the lambdas of **all** queries together, choosing splits by least squares.
3. Set each leaf's value with one Newton step (below).
4. Add the tree times a learning rate $\eta$ to every row's score.

blocks.caption: Burges Section 7. Here lambda_i is the signed push (positive means up) and w_i is the second derivative of the LambdaRank utility, so the leaf value is a Newton step.

blocks.title: What the first tree is trained on

scenes.caption: Each document has two features. To keep the arithmetic visible, the tree is a stump (one split, two leaves) and there is just this one query.
The regression target is the lambda from the LambdaRank lesson, not the label. B and C want to go up, A and D down.
Click-through rate already separates them: A and D have CTR at most 0.05, B and C at least 0.22. A split on CTR between 0.05 and 0.22 should fit the targets well.

blocks.title: Squared error of each candidate split

scenes.caption: Every threshold between adjacent feature values is a candidate. For each, the leaves predict the mean lambda of their rows and we add up the squared errors.
The winner is CTR <= 0.135 with squared error 0.0607, splitting {A, D} from {B, C}. BM25 <= 2.6 and CTR <= 0.26 tie at 0.0949: both isolate B.

blocks.title: The fitted stump and its Newton leaf values

nodes.label:
new score = old
+ 0.1 x leaf value

scenes.caption: The split chosen by least squares on the lambdas.
Newton step per leaf. Left: -0.3872 / 0.1175 = -3.2952. Right: +0.3872 / 0.1514 = +2.5575. The leaf sums are equal and opposite because all lambdas of a query sum to zero.
With learning rate 0.1, A and D move by -0.3295 and B and C by +0.2557.

blocks.prompt: After this first tree (learning rate 0.1), A's score falls from 2.0 to 1.670 and B's rises from 1.0 to 1.256. Does NDCG improve?
blocks.reveal: No. NDCG is still 0.6590, because A is still above B; the gap shrank from 1.0 to 0.415. The second tree (again a CTR split) brings A to 1.425 and B to 1.450, B passes A, and NDCG jumps to 0.9639. Many small steps accumulate until the order flips; NDCG only reports the flips.

scenes.caption: Round 0: the starting scores. Order A, B, C, D, NDCG 0.6590.
After tree 1: same order, NDCG still 0.6590, but A and B are now 0.415 apart instead of 1.0. D goes negative (shown by bar height; its sign is in the label).
After tree 2: B (1.450) passes A (1.425). Order B, A, C, D and NDCG 0.9639. Getting C above A too needs more trees and richer splits.

blocks.title: The LambdaMART training loop
blocks.code:
F = base_scores(X)        # or 0 for every row
for m in range(n_trees):
    lam, w = [], []
    for q in queries:          # per query group
        order = sort_by(F[q])
        l, h = lambdas_and_weights(q, order)
        lam += l; w += h
    tree = fit_regression_tree(X, lam, leaves=L)
    for leaf in tree.leaves:   # Newton step
        leaf.value = sum(lam[leaf]) / sum(w[leaf])
    F += eta * tree.predict(X)

scenes.caption: Start from a base model's scores (Burges notes this allows model adaptation) or from zero.
Lambdas are computed per query after sorting by current scores, because |delta NDCG| depends on positions.
One tree is fit to the lambdas of all queries at once, so a split must work across queries. That only works because features like CTR mean the same thing in every query.
Newton step per leaf, then add the tree scaled by eta.

blocks.md: Simplified for teaching: one query and a stump with least-squares splits, as in Burges's description. LightGBM and XGBoost grow deeper trees from millions of rows and choose splits with a gain computed from summed gradients and hessians, and LightGBM also rescales the pushes per query when lambdarank_norm is on. The mechanism, fitting trees to lambdas, is the same.
LambdaMART = gradient boosted regression trees whose regression targets are the LambdaRank lambdas, recomputed after re-sorting at every round.

blocks.question: The Newton leaf value for B and C was +2.557, yet we only added +0.256. Why use a learning rate below 1?
options: Because taking smaller steps than the locally optimal one acts as regularization and usually improves test accuracy
Because the Newton step is always wrong in sign
Because NDCG is bounded by 1
Because the lambdas must sum to zero
blocks.explain: Burges: a step smaller than the optimal one acts as regularization that can significantly improve test accuracy. The lambdas are also recomputed after each tree, so a huge step would be based on stale positions.

blocks.question: Which statement about what one LambdaMART tree learns is correct?
options: It predicts each document's relevance label
It predicts NDCG for each query
It predicts the per-document lambdas from the features, pooled over all queries
It learns a separate tree for each query
blocks.explain: The regression targets are the lambdas, and Burges stresses that each tree models the lambdas for the entire dataset, not a single query. Labels enter only through |delta NDCG|.

lessons.title: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias

blocks.md:
Both major gradient boosting libraries ship LambdaMART. In LightGBM, `LGBMRanker` defaults to `objective="lambdarank"`. In XGBoost the default ranking objective is `rank:ndcg`, which the docs describe as LambdaMART; `rank:pairwise` is the RankNet objective and `rank:map` swaps in mean average precision.

Both need to know where each query group starts and ends, and both expect rows sorted by query.

blocks.code:
import lightgbm as lgb

# rows sorted by query; group = rows per query, sum(group) == len(X)
ranker = lgb.LGBMRanker(
    objective="lambdarank",
    n_estimators=500,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    label_gain=[0, 1, 3, 7, 15],       # gain per integer label 0..4
    lambdarank_truncation_level=20,
)
ranker.fit(X_train, y_train, group=[10, 20, 40, 10, 10, 10],
           eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], eval_group=[val_groups],
           eval_at=[5, 10])
scores = ranker.predict(X_candidates)   # sort descending to rank
blocks.caption: LightGBM. The group example is the one from the LGBMRanker docs: 6 queries over 100 rows.

blocks.code:
import xgboost as xgb

# qid must be sorted in non-decreasing order
ranker = xgb.XGBRanker(
    objective="rank:ndcg",
    lambdarank_pair_method="topk",
    lambdarank_num_pair_per_sample=10,   # truncation level for topk
    n_estimators=500,
)
ranker.fit(X_train, y_train, qid=qid_train)
blocks.caption: XGBoost. Labels are graded integers; qid gives the query of each row.

blocks.md:
The knobs map directly onto the formulas you computed:

- **label_gain** (LightGBM): the gain of each integer label. The default is 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, ... (that is $2^l - 1$), and every label must be smaller than the number of entries. XGBoost's `ndcg_exp_gain` (default true) chooses the same exponential gain.
- **Truncation**: LightGBM's `lambdarank_truncation_level` (default 30) only forms pairs in which at least one document is within that many top positions of the current sorted list. XGBoost's `topk` pair method (the default) does the same with `lambdarank_num_pair_per_sample` as the level.
- **Normalization**: `lambdarank_norm` (LightGBM, default true) normalizes lambdas per query for unbalanced data, the query-imbalance problem from the pairwise lesson.
- **eval_at**: NDCG positions to report; LightGBM defaults to 1 to 5.

blocks.prompt: You set `lambdarank_truncation_level=3`, but users scroll through 10 results. Predict the effect on ranks 4 to 10.
blocks.reveal: Pairs where both documents sit below position 3 in the current sorted list produce no lambdas, so the model gets no signal for ordering positions 4 to 10 among themselves. A pair still counts if one of its documents is in the top 3. Set the truncation level at least as deep as the positions you care about, or deeper.

blocks.md: **Where labels come from.** Human judgments are expensive, so many systems train on clicks. But clicks are biased by **position**: people examine top results more often. Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel (WSDM 2017) model a click as happening when a result is **examined** and **relevant**, with an examination probability, the **propensity**, that depends on rank. Weighting each click by 1 over its propensity (inverse propensity scoring, IPS) gives an unbiased estimate of the loss you would get from true relevance.

blocks.caption: Joachims et al., Eq. 5: for each logged query, each clicked result contributes its rank under the new ranker S, divided by the propensity of the position where it was shown.

blocks.title: Correcting position bias with propensity weights

scenes.caption: Two equally relevant results over 100 impressions. Suppose examination probability is 1/rank (the power law Joachims et al. used to simulate clicks with eta = 1): X at rank 1 is always examined, Y at rank 4 a quarter of the time.
Expected clicks if users click whenever they examine a relevant result: X gets 100 and Y 25. Trained on raw clicks, the model learns X is four times better.
IPS divides each click by its propensity: 100 / 1 = 100 and 25 / 0.25 = 100. The two are equal again, as their true relevance is.

blocks.md: In practice the propensities are estimated, not assumed. Joachims et al. swapped the top result with a result at a random rank and compared click-through rates, since only ratios of propensities are needed. Libraries now include debiasing: XGBoost's `lambdarank_unbiased` (experimental) implements Unbiased LambdaMART (Hu et al., WWW 2019), and LightGBM's lambdarank can model position bias when positions are provided, with `lambdarank_position_bias_regularization`.

IPS only works where the propensity is above zero. A relevant document that was never shown, or shown where nobody ever looks, gets no clicks at all and cannot be recovered by reweighting; Joachims et al. state the estimate is unbiased only if the propensity is positive for every relevant result.

In production, LambdaMART is the training objective of a tree ensemble that rescores the top candidates of a first-stage retriever. Its quality depends on labels (judgments or debiased clicks), query-grouped data, and a truncation level that matches the positions users see.

blocks.question: Your LightGBM ranker fails with an error about labels after you switch to a 0 to 10 relevance scale. What is the likely cause?
options: LambdaRank only supports binary labels
group sizes must be equal
label_gain was set to five values, and every label must be smaller than the number of label_gain entries
eval_at must include 10
blocks.explain: LightGBM looks up each label's gain in label_gain, so labels must be smaller than its length. The default list has 31 entries, but a custom five-entry list only supports labels 0 to 4.

blocks.question: Result Z was shown at a position with estimated propensity 0.2 and was clicked 30 times over the logged queries. What total IPS weight do those clicks contribute?
blocks.explain: Each click is weighted by 1 / 0.2 = 5, so 30 clicks count as 150. Clicks at rarely examined positions count more because they reveal relevance that is usually hidden.

blocks.question: Which change makes XGBoost optimize mean average precision instead of NDCG while keeping the LambdaMART machinery?
options: objective="rank:pairwise"
lambdarank_pair_method="mean"
ndcg_exp_gain=False
objective="rank:map"
blocks.explain: rank:map uses LambdaMART with the change in MAP in place of the change in NDCG, the substitution Burges describes. rank:pairwise is plain RankNet, with no metric weighting.
